title: When a drug is adulterated under 21 U.S.C. 351
rule_summary: Under 21 U.S.C. 351 a drug is deemed adulterated, among other grounds: (a)(1) if it consists in whole or in part of any filthy, putrid, or decomposed substance; (a)(2)(A) if it has been prepared, packed, or held under insanitary conditions whereby it may have been contaminated with filth, or whereby it may have been rendered injurious to health; (a)(2)(B) if the methods used in, or the facilities or controls used for, its manufacture, processing, packing, or holding do not conform to current good manufacturing practice to assure that it meets the requirements as to safety and has the identity and strength, and meets the quality and purity characteristics, which it purports or is represented to possess; (a)(3) if its container is composed, in whole or in part, of any poisonous or deleterious substance which may render the contents injurious to health; (b) if it purports to be or is represented as a drug recognized in an official compendium and its strength differs from, or its quality or purity falls below, the compendial standard; (c) if it is not subject to (b) and its strength differs from, or its purity or quality falls below, that which it purports or is represented to possess; and (d) if any substance has been mixed or packed with it so as to reduce its quality or strength or substituted wholly or in part for it.
exam_relevance: Tests the adulteration grounds, which describe what is wrong with the product itself or how it was prepared, packed or held, as distinct from misbranding, which concerns labeling and packaging.

authority.name: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act

common_confusions: Holding under insanitary conditions whereby the drug may have been contaminated or rendered injurious to health is enough under 351(a)(2)(A); actual contamination need not be shown.
Adulteration concerns the drug's composition, strength, quality, purity or conditions of preparation, packing or holding; false or misleading labeling is misbranding.
